In [[mathematics]], a [[sequence]] of [[vector space|vector]]s (''x''<sub>''n''</sub>) in a [[Hilbert space]] <math>(H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)</math> is called a '''Riesz sequence''' if there exist [[constant (mathematics)|constants]] <math>0<c\le C<\infty</math> such that 
<math display="block"> c \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} | a_n|^2  \leq \left\Vert \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n x_n \right\Vert^2 \leq C \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} | a_n|^2, </math>
for every finite [[scalar (mathematics)|scalar]] sequence <math>\{a_n\}</math> and hence, for all <math>\{a_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\in \ell^{2}</math>.{{sfn|Christensen|2016|pp=89-92}}{{sfn|Balazs|Stoeva|Antoine|2010|p=3}}

A Riesz sequence is called a '''Riesz [[Basis (linear algebra)|basis]]''' if
<math display="block">\overline{\mathop{\rm span} (x_n)} = H.</math>
Equivalently, a Riesz basis for <math>H</math> is a family of the form <math> \left\{x_{n} \right\}_{n=1}^{\infty} = \left\{ Ue_{n} \right\}_{n=1}^{\infty} </math>, where <math> \left\{e_{n} \right\}_{n=1}^{\infty} </math> is an [[orthonormal basis]] for <math> H </math> and <math> U : H \rightarrow H </math> is a bounded bijective operator. Subsequently, there exist constants <math>0<c\leq C < \infty</math> such that{{sfn|Christensen|2016|pp=86-87}}
<math display="block"> c \|f\|^2  \leq  \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} |\langle f, x_n \rangle|^2 \leq C \|f\|^2, \quad \forall f \in H.</math> 
Hence, Riesz bases need not be orthonormal, i.e., they are a generalization of orthonormal bases.{{sfn | Antoine | Balazs | 2012}}

== Paley-Wiener criterion ==
{{distinguish|Paley-Wiener theorem}}
Let <math> \{e_{n}\} </math> be an orthonormal basis for a Hilbert space <math> H </math> and let <math> \{x_{n}\} </math>  be "close" to <math> \{e_{n}\} </math> in the sense that 

:<math> \left\| \sum a_{i} (e_{i} - x_{i})\right\| \leq \lambda \sqrt{\sum |a_{i}|^{2}} </math> 

for some constant <math> \lambda </math>, <math> 0 \leq \lambda < 1 </math>, and arbitrary scalars <math> a_{1},\dotsc, a_{n} </math> <math> (n = 1,2,3,\dotsc) </math> . Then <math> \{x_{n}\} </math> is a Riesz basis for <math> H </math>.{{sfn | Young | 2001 | p=35}}{{sfn | Paley | Wiener | 1934 | p=100}}

==Theorems==
If ''H'' is a [[dimension (vector space)|finite-dimensional]] space, then every basis of ''H'' is a Riesz basis.

Let <math>\varphi</math> be in the [[Lp space|''L''<sup>''p''</sup> space]] ''L''<sup>2</sup>('''R'''), let

:<math>\varphi_n(x) = \varphi(x-n)</math>

and let <math>\hat{\varphi}</math> denote the [[Fourier transform]] of <math>{\varphi}</math>.  Define constants ''c'' and ''C'' with <math>0<c\le C<+\infty</math>.  Then the following are equivalent:{{sfn|Hernandez|Weiss|1996|loc=chpt. 2.1 Multiresolution analysis}}

:<math>1. \quad \forall (a_n) \in \ell^2,\ \ c\left( \sum_n | a_n|^2 \right) \leq \left\Vert \sum_n a_n \varphi_n \right\Vert^2 \leq C \left( \sum_n | a_n|^2 \right)</math>

:<math>2. \quad c\leq\sum_{n}\left|\hat{\varphi}(\omega + 2\pi n)\right|^2\leq C</math>

The first of the above conditions is the definition for (<math>{\varphi_n}</math>) to form a Riesz basis for the space it [[linear span|span]]s.

== Kadec 1/4 Theorem ==
{{see also|Frame (linear algebra)#Non-harmonic Fourier series}}
The '''[[Mikhail Kadets|Kadec]] 1/4 theorem''', sometimes called the '''Kadets 1/4 theorem''', provides a specific condition under which a sequence of [[complex exponential]]s forms a Riesz basis for the [[Lp space]] <math>L^2[-\pi, \pi]</math>. It is a foundational result in the theory of non-harmonic Fourier series.

Let <math>\Lambda = \{\lambda_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}</math> be a sequence of real numbers such that
:<math> \sup_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |\lambda_n - n| < \frac{1}{4} </math>
Then the sequence of complex exponentials <math>\{e^{i \lambda_n t}\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}</math> forms a Riesz basis for <math>L^2[-\pi, \pi]</math>.{{sfn | Young | 2001 | p=36}}

This theorem demonstrates the stability of the standard orthonormal basis <math>\{e^{int}\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} </math> (up to normalization) under perturbations of the frequencies <math>n</math>.

The constant 1/4 is sharp; if <math>\sup_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |\lambda_n - n| = 1/4</math>, the sequence may fail to be a Riesz basis, such as:{{sfn|Young|2001|p=37}}<math display="block">\lambda_n= \begin{cases}n-\frac{1}{4}, & n>0 \\ 0, & n=0 \\ n+\frac{1}{4}, & n<0\end{cases}</math>When <math>\Lambda = \{\lambda_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}</math> are allowed to be complex, the theorem holds under the condition <math> \sup_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |\lambda_n - n| < \frac{\log 2}{\pi} </math>. Whether the constant is sharp is an open question.{{sfn|Young|2001|p=37}}
